title: First Sunday of Advent (Mark 13:33–37)
hook: the new year starts with watch

segments.voice: Yesterday, the key to the calendar: solemnities, feasts, memorials, and Sunday at the center. Your line was every day has a rank. What rank did your day turn out to have? Day six hundred thirty-three.

New Year's Eve has a countdown and a party. The Church's new year begins on a Sunday in late November or early December, in purple, with a single candle and a warning. No fireworks. The first gospel of the year is not a birth story. It's about a house at night, a master who has gone away, and a doorkeeper told to stay awake. In the year when Mark's Gospel is read on Sundays, these five verses, Mark 13:33 to 37, open everything. Today the year turns over, and its first word is a command.
screen: `A NEW YEAR IN PURPLE.` → `A HOUSE AT NIGHT.` → `THE FIRST WORD IS A COMMAND.`

segments.voice: Advent comes from the Latin adventus, a coming or an arrival. Across the Sundays before Christmas, the Church looks two ways at once: back to the first coming, the birth in Bethlehem, and forward to the coming at the end of time. The first Sunday leans hard forward. In Mark, Jesus tells a small story. A man goes on a long journey. He leaves his house in his servants' hands, gives each one a job, and tells the porter at the door to keep watch. Nobody knows when he'll be back: in the evening, at midnight, at cockcrow, or in the morning. Four times, named one after another, so every hour of the dark is covered. Don't let him come suddenly and find you sleeping. Then the last line, which Mark aims past the disciples at every reader: "And what I say to you, I say to all: Watch." The Greek word is grēgoreite, stay awake, keep alert. It's a word for staying up when sleep would be easier. Notice what it doesn't say. It doesn't say panic, or calculate the date, or stare at the sky. Each servant has work. Watching, in this story, looks like doing your job well while staying awake to who might walk through the door. That's why the Church starts its year here. Before the manger, before the shepherds and the star, the first thing asked is attention. Then on this Sunday, in some homes, someone lights the first of four candles on a wreath, and the room has one small flame against the dark.
screen: `ADVENT: A COMING.` · `THE MASTER GOES AWAY.` · `FOUR WATCHES OF THE NIGHT.` · `WATCHING LOOKS LIKE WORK.` · then, large: `WHAT I SAY TO YOU, I SAY TO ALL: WATCH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: light one candle. If you have an Advent wreath, light the first candle. If not, any candle will do, or a single lamp in a dark room. Sit where you can see the flame. Watch it the way a doorkeeper watches a door: awake, unhurried, ready. When your mind wanders, come back to the light. If you pray, you can say the old word of Advent, take the water of life, freely. If you don't, just keep watch with the flame. The bell holds the time.
Gregoreite, stay awake. Mark thirteen: the Church's new year begins with a house at night and a porter told to keep watch. Today's word.
Your line: watch. Today, at one ordinary task, stay fully awake to it, and to whoever walks through your door. Day six hundred thirty-three.

howItsDone: On the First Sunday of Advent, Catholic churches begin the new liturgical year in violet vestments, and many parishes and families light the first candle of an Advent wreath.

trapdoor: what you thought: Advent is the Christmas shopping season.
what it means: the weeks of waiting that open the Church's year, looking back to Bethlehem and forward to Christ's return.
what a scholar hears: Mark names four night watches, evening to morning, and ends: what I say to you, I say to all, grēgoreite.

notes: Mark 13:33–37 is the gospel of the First Sunday of Advent in Year B. Confirm.
Four watches (evening, midnight, cockcrow, morning) as the Roman division of the night. Confirm phrasing.
Advent wreath: widely traced to 19th-century German Protestant practice and later adopted by Catholics; not stated in the script. Keeper may add.
Greek γρηγορεῖτε in Mark 13:37 and its pronunciation; confirm.
Advent as the start of the liturgical year falls between Nov 27 and Dec 3. Confirm.
Editor review (2026-10-01): cut the unsourced 'Roman' night-watch claim (hook, teach, trapdoor), 'four weeks' (Advent can be shorter) and two sweeping 'most/many' lines.
